School

Africana Philosophy quotes

Africana philosophy names philosophical work from Africa and the African diaspora—written critique, conceptual analysis, and political thought—rather than a single folk worldview.

52 passages · 9 voices in this archive selection

Overview

Modern debates distinguish ethnophilosophy from professional philosophy (Hountondji), pursue conceptual decolonization (Wiredu), reclaim agency under colonialism (Fanon, Césaire), and articulate cosmopolitan ethics (Appiah). Ubuntu-related work (e.g. Ramose) treats communal personhood carefully as philosophy, not slogan.

Historical notes

Early modern figures such as Anton Wilhelm Amo sit beside twentieth-century Négritude and postcolonial critique. The archive’s Africana passages emphasize verifiable texts over invented ancient Egyptian ‘quotations.’

Core ideas

  • African philosophy exists as literature and argument, not only as collective myth.
  • Conceptual decolonization asks which categories travel and which distort.
  • Colonialism damages both the colonized and the colonizer’s humanity.
  • Personhood and community (Ubuntu debates) repay careful philosophical treatment.

FAQ

What is Africana philosophy?

It is philosophy produced in African and diaspora contexts—texts, arguments, and concepts—across ethics, politics, language, and method.

Who are major Africana philosophers in this archive?

Kwasi Wiredu, Paulin Hountondji, Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Kwame Anthony Appiah, Léopold Sédar Senghor, Anton Wilhelm Amo, and Mogobe B. Ramose, among others.

Where can I find Africana philosophy quotes?
